hallmark: the skull on the thorax, and the banded abdomen with its grey dorsal stripe

reference.title: British and European Butterflies and Moths (Macrolepidoptera), plate XIII figure 1

doc: *Acherontia atropos*, upperside, wings spread — the death's-head hawkmoth.
Traced from figure 1 of plate XIII of Kirby's *British and European
Butterflies and Moths*, the same book and the same hands as the peacock two
accessions earlier. `references/acherontia-atropos.jpg` is the plate; the
moth is the upper figure and 1a is its larva.
Unlike the peacock, this figure is drawn square to the page and symmetric,
so the proportions came off it directly: 425 pixels from the front of the
head to the tip of the abdomen, 122 units across the thorax and a half-span
of 1150 — which is 1.15 body lengths, and matches the animal's 90 to 130
millimetres of wing against 55 of body.
## What the drawing has to get right
The **skull**, obviously. It is a real marking and not a trick of the light:
a pale patch on the thorax with two dark sockets in it and a dark vertical
mouth below, and it is the reason the animal has been an omen in three
languages. Drawn as those three shapes clipped to the thorax — the pale
ground, the pair of sockets, the mouth — because one shape would be a patch
and the arrangement is the whole thing.
Then the **abdomen**, which is the other half of the identification: broad,
banded across, and split lengthwise by a wide grey-blue dorsal stripe. Six
bands and a stripe, and the stripe drawn on the axis where it belongs.
Then the **hindwing bands**. Two dark bands on an orange ground, both
following the outer margin, and they are drawn as three strips on one traced
edge at three depths — dark to 96, pigment over it to 52, dark again over
that to 20. What shows is band, ground, band. Offsetting three edges by hand
instead would put each of them a few units wrong all the way round.
## No legs
A hawkmoth at rest holds its legs under the thorax and a spread figure shows
none, which is why `REQUIRED_PARTS.lepidoptera` does not ask for them. The
palps are drawn, because a Sphingid's are large, upturned and visible from
above.
## Plate space
y = 0 at the front of the head, y = 1000 at the tip of the abdomen. The
forewing apex is at x = 1150, and the antennae reach above y = -180.

note: The hind wing first, so the forewing overlaps its base — which is the way
round a spread moth is put together and the reason the orange only shows
below the forewing's trailing edge.
The two dark bands, as three strips on one edge.
Deepest first: dark to 96 units in from the margin, the orange ground
over it to 52, dark again over that to 20. What is left showing is a
narrow band at the margin, the ground, and a second band inside — which
is what the reference has, and it is one measured edge rather than three.
The fore wing: long, narrow and pointed, swept back from a costa that is
nearly straight. A hawkmoth's wing is built for a hundred kilometres of
migration and it looks like it — this animal reaches Britain from north
Africa under its own power.
The transverse fasciae — the paler zigzag bands across the forewing. Four
strokes, from a guide near the wing base to one out towards the apex.
Kirby's lithograph carries them as mottling in three or four browns. An
engraving has line and nothing else, so what is kept is where the bands
run and not what colour they are.
The two pale flecks near the middle of each forewing. Small, and drawn
because they are the only two hard-edged marks on a wing that is
otherwise all gradation.
The abdomen. Broad and heavy — a hawkmoth carries the flight muscle and
the fuel for it — with the bands across and the grey dorsal stripe down.
The bands, as seven strokes each crossing the axis — the fan case the
validator allows on the midline, because both guides are centred on it.
The strokes narrow as they go back, which is the abdomen tapering rather
than the bands changing.
The dorsal stripe: broad, grey-blue on the animal, and the reason the
bands read as bands rather than as rings. Drawn on the axis and once.
The thorax, furred and heavy, and the surface the skull is on.
The skull: the pale ground, then the two sockets, then the mouth.
Three shapes rather than one, because a single pale oval on a moth's back
is a pale oval. What makes it a skull is that there are two dark spots
high in it and one dark mark low and central, and a reader's eye does the
rest — which is exactly what the moth is relying on.
A palp. Large, upturned and scaled, and one of the few Sphingid
characters that shows from above — which is why `palp` is in
`PLATE_PART_IDS` at all and this is the first plate to use it.
The antenna: stout at the base and tapering to a fine point, which is a
hawkmoth's and is why the record says `filiform` where the peacock says
`clavate`. Three joints, drawn heavier than any other antenna here.
